subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Herpes simplex viruses (HSV‑1, HSV‑2) are DNA viruses that cause mucocutaneous lesions, neonatal disease and encephalitis. They establish latency in sensory ganglia and reactivate under stress or immunosuppression.

sections.p: HSV are enveloped, double‑stranded DNA viruses of the Herpesviridae family. They infect epithelial cells, then travel retrograde to sensory ganglia where they persist as latent genomes.
b: Two main types: HSV‑1 (oral/ocular, also genital) and HSV‑2 (genital, neonatal).
Latency in trigeminal (HSV‑1) or sacral (HSV‑2) ganglia.

sections.p: The virion contains a capsid, tegument and glycoprotein‑rich envelope that mediates entry via heparan sulfate receptors.
b: Enveloped DNA virus; sensitive to drying, heat, detergents.
Glycoproteins gD, gB, gC essential for attachment and fusion.

sections.p: HSV spreads by direct contact with infected secretions or lesions. After replication in epithelium, virions travel to sensory neurons, establish latency, and reactivate when immunity wanes.
b: Oral contact → HSV‑1; sexual contact → HSV‑2.
Neonatal infection via birth canal (HSV‑2) or post‑natal contact (HSV‑1).

sections.p: Clinical manifestations range from mild mucocutaneous vesicles to severe encephalitis and disseminated neonatal disease.
b: Primary oral herpes: painful vesicles → ulceration on lips/face (HSV‑1).
Genital herpes: grouped vesicles → shallow ulcers (HSV‑2, occasional HSV‑1).
Herpes encephalitis: fever, headache, focal deficits, seizures (HSV‑1).
Neonatal HSV: skin, eye, mouth disease; disseminated organ involvement; high mortality without therapy.

sections.p: Laboratory confirmation relies on direct detection of virus or its DNA, especially when clinical picture is atypical.

t.b: Does the lesion contain multinucleated giant cells? Positive result supports HSV but cannot differentiate HSV‑1 vs HSV‑2.

t.a: PCR from lesion swab or CSF
t.b: Is HSV DNA present? Positive result confirms infection; quantitative PCR helps monitor viral load in encephalitis.
Can live virus be grown? Useful where PCR unavailable; slower and less sensitive.
Has the patient seroconverted? IgM indicates recent infection; IgG indicates past exposure, helpful in neonates.

sections.p: Antiviral therapy targets viral DNA polymerase; early treatment reduces morbidity and mortality.
b: Acyclovir (IV for encephalitis, oral for mucocutaneous disease) – selective toxicity via viral thymidine kinase.
Valacyclovir and famciclovir – oral prodrugs with better bioavailability.
Suppressive therapy (daily acyclovir/valacyclovir) for frequent recurrences or HIV co‑infection.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and clinical practice.
b: HSV‑1 is the leading cause of sporadic encephalitis; treat empirically with IV acyclovir before PCR result.
Neonatal HSV presents as skin‑eye‑mouth disease, disseminated disease, or CNS disease – all need IV acyclovir.
Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells but cannot type HSV; confirm with PCR.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly spreading facial or genital lesions with fever
New onset seizures, altered mental status, or focal neurologic deficits (possible encephalitis)
Neonatal vesicular rash, lethargy, or organ dysfunction

faq.a: No; antivirals suppress replication, but the virus remains latent for life.

faq.q: Why is HSV‑1 more common in encephalitis than HSV‑2?
faq.a: HSV‑1 preferentially travels to the temporal lobe via trigeminal pathways, causing encephalitis.

faq.q: Is a negative Tzanck smear enough to rule out HSV?
faq.a: No; sensitivity is low. PCR is preferred when suspicion remains.

exam: Describe the pathogenesis of HSV latency and reactivation.
List the diagnostic steps for suspected HSV encephalitis and interpret a positive PCR result.
Explain why acyclovir is preferred for HSV treatment and why dosing adjustments are needed in renal impairment.
